## 0. How to use this tutorial

Part 1 drew life expectancy over time with lines and paths. This part makes the graph move: one frame for each year. We use the package `gganimate`, which adds an animation to a `ggplot` graph.

Work through the steps in order. Every step has the same parts:

1.  **Question.** Read it.
2.  **Predict.** Write your guess in one line before you run any code.
3.  **Your code.** Write the code in the empty chunk, remove `#| eval: false` and run it.
4.  **Your finding.** Write what you see in one sentence.
5.  **Solution.** Open the grey box and compare. The box is closed on purpose: try first.

An animation takes a few seconds to render. Wait for it to finish.

## 1. Packages

```{r}
#| label: install-pacman
if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("pacman")
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, here, 
               ggrepel,      # labels that do not overlap
               gganimate,    # adds animation to a ggplot graph
               gifski,       # builds the animation file (a gif)
               plotly)       # interactive graphs for HTML, used in Step 10
```

## 2. Datasets

Each dataset loads once into a named object.

```{r}
#| label: data
life_wide <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sergiouribe/Data_Visualization_Course_RSU/main/data/gapminder_life_expectancy_wide.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

continents <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sergiouribe/Data_Visualization_Course_RSU/main/data/countries_continents_codes.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

rosling <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sergiouribe/Data_Visualization_Course_RSU/main/data/rosling_tidy.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

`life_wide` has one column per year for 194 countries. `continents` has the continent of each country. `rosling` has life expectancy, income and population of 142 countries every 5 years from 1952 to 2007.

## 3. Prepare the table

Run this chunk once. It builds the table `life_long` with one row per country and year, as in part 1. Each function has one job:

-   `pivot_longer()` turns the year columns into rows. `-c(geo, name)` keeps the columns `geo` and `name` as they are.
-   `as.integer()` turns the year, which is text after pivoting, into a whole number.
-   `left_join()` adds the columns of a second table, matching rows with the same `geo`.
-   `transmute()` works like `mutate()` and keeps only the columns you create. Here it builds a small table with `geo` and `continent`.
-   `str_to_lower()` writes text in lower case, so "LVA" becomes "lva" and the codes of both tables match.
-   `head()` prints the first 6 rows.

```{r}
#| label: prepare
life_long <- life_wide |>
  pivot_longer(-c(geo, name), 
               names_to = "year", 
               values_to = "life_exp") |>                 # years in columns become rows
  mutate(year = as.integer(year)) |>                      # the year is text after pivoting, make it a number
  filter(year <= 2023) |>                                 # drop the projections after 2023
  left_join(
    continents |>
      transmute(geo = str_to_lower(`alpha-3`),            # the codes in life_wide are in lower case
                continent = region),
    by = "geo"
  )

life_long |> 
  head()
```

## 4. Animate a line

### Step 1: A line that grows

**Question.** Can the line of each Baltic country draw itself year by year?

Start from the static graph of part 1: filter Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania from 1900 to 1960, put `year` on `x`, `life_exp` on `y` and `color = name`, and draw `geom_line()`. Then add `transition_reveal(year)`. The function `transition_reveal()` shows the line up to the current year and extends it frame by frame. Add `labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_along)}")` to print the year. The text in `{ }` is replaced in each frame, and `frame_along` is the year of the current frame. The function `round()` rounds it to a whole number, because many frames fall between two years.

**Predict.** Which line will fall first?

```{r}
#| label: a1
#| eval: false
life_long |>
```

**Your finding:**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
#| label: a1-solution
life_long |>
  filter(name %in% c("Estonia", "Latvia", "Lithuania"), 
         year >= 1900, year <= 1960) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, 
             y = life_exp, 
             color = name)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_along)}",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       color = NULL) +
  transition_reveal(year)       # the line grows from left to right, one frame for each step
```

The three lines rise together until 1914 and fall in 1915 to 1918. In 1941 the Lithuanian line drops to 12.2 years, and in 1944 Latvia reaches 26.8 years and Estonia 35.2 years.
:::

### Step 2: Add a moving point at the tip

**Question.** How do we show where the line is now?

Add `geom_point()` to the chart of Step 1. During `transition_reveal()`, a point is drawn only for the current frame, so it moves along the tip of each line.

**Predict.** Does the point show a value that the line already passed?

```{r}
#| label: a2
#| eval: false
life_long |>
```

**Your finding:**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
#| label: a2-solution
life_long |>
  filter(name %in% c("Estonia", "Latvia", "Lithuania"), 
         year >= 1900, year <= 1960) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, 
             y = life_exp, 
             color = name)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 3) +          # one point at the tip of each line
  labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_along)}",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       color = NULL) +
  transition_reveal(year)
```

The point sits at the current year. It shows the value of that frame, and the line behind it shows the past.
:::

### Check 1

What is the difference between `transition_reveal(year)` and `transition_time(year)`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`transition_reveal(year)` keeps all earlier values on the graph and extends the line, so it fits lines and paths. `transition_time(year)` shows only the rows of the current year, so the points move and nothing stays behind unless you add `shadow_mark()`. Steps 3 to 5 use it.
:::

## 5. Animate the trail of the Rosling graph

### Step 3: The animated trail

**Question.** How do six countries move year by year? Poland and Sweden represent Europe, where this course takes place. Chile and the United States represent the Americas. Nigeria is the country with most people in Africa and China is the country with most people in Asia.

Take the six countries (`rosling`, `income` on `x` on a log scale with `scale_x_log10()`, which spaces the axis by multiples of 10 so that poor and rich countries both fit on the graph, `life_exp` on `y`, `color = country`) and draw `geom_point(size = 3)`. Add `transition_time(year)`: each frame shows the rows of one year, so the points move. The year is stored in `frame_time`, so write `labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}")`. Then add `shadow_mark(past = TRUE, alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5)`. The function `shadow_mark()` keeps the positions of the earlier frames on the graph. `past = TRUE` keeps the past, `alpha = 0.4` makes the old points transparent and `size = 1.5` makes them small. The old points form the trail.

**Predict.** Which country moves backwards at some point?

```{r}
#| label: a3
#| eval: false
rosling |>
```

**Your finding:**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
#| label: a3-solution
rosling |>
  filter(country %in% c("Poland", "Sweden", "Chile", "United States", "Nigeria", "China")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, 
             y = life_exp, 
             color = country)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +                                   # the current position
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}",
       x = "Income per person (log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       color = NULL) +
  transition_time(year) +                                  # one frame for each year
  shadow_mark(past = TRUE, alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5)        # the old positions stay as a trail
```

China moves backwards in 1962: life expectancy falls from 50.5 to 44.5 years. Nigeria rises from 36.3 to 46.9 years in 55 years. Sweden starts at 71.9 years and ends at 80.9 years, a gain of 9.0 years, while Poland gains 14.3 years (61.3 to 75.6). Sweden and the United States start on the right side of the graph and stay there for the whole period.
:::

### Step 4: Make all the countries move

**Question.** What does the animation show when we draw every country?

Use `transition_time(year)` as in Step 3: each frame shows the countries of one year. Use all 142 countries, `size = population`, `color = continent` and `geom_point(alpha = 0.7)`. Add `scale_size(range = c(1, 12), guide = "none")` to set the size of the points and hide the size legend, `scale_color_viridis_d()` for the colours (the viridis palette, readable with colour blindness), and `labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}")`. With `transition_time()` the year is stored in `frame_time`.

**Predict.** Which continent moves furthest to the right?

```{r}
#| label: a4
#| eval: false
rosling |>
```

**Your finding:**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
#| label: a4-solution
rosling |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, 
             y = life_exp, 
             color = continent, 
             size = population)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_size(range = c(1, 12), guide = "none") +      # point sizes from 1 to 12, no size legend
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}",
       x = "Income per person (log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       color = "Continent") +
  transition_time(year)                                # one frame for each year, R fills the steps in between
```

All continents move up and to the right between 1952 and 2007. Europe starts at a median income of 5,142 and ends at 28,054. Africa starts at 987 and ends at 1,452.
:::

### Step 5: Leave a trail behind the points

**Question.** How do we see the path that each country took?

Add `shadow_wake(wake_length = 0.1)` after `transition_time(year)`. The function `shadow_wake()` draws copies of the points from the last frames, which fade out. `wake_length = 0.1` sets the tail to 10% of the animation.

**Predict.** Does a short or a long tail show the movement better?

```{r}
#| label: a5
#| eval: false
rosling |>
```

**Your finding:**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
#| label: a5-solution
rosling |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, 
             y = life_exp, 
             color = continent, 
             size = population)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_size(range = c(1, 12), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}",
       x = "Income per person (log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       color = "Continent") +
  transition_time(year) +
  shadow_wake(wake_length = 0.1)                       # a fading tail behind each point
```

The tail shows the direction and the speed of each country. Long tails mark fast movement, such as China.
:::

### Step 6: One panel for each continent

**Question.** How does each continent move, when we separate them?

Add `facet_wrap(~ continent)` to the graph of Step 4. The function `facet_wrap()` draws one small panel for each value of `continent`, and the animation runs in all panels at the same time. The colour now repeats the panel name, so hide it with `scale_color_viridis_d(guide = "none")`. Use `scale_size(range = c(1, 8), guide = "none")` to keep the points small in small panels.

**Predict.** In which panel do the points move furthest to the right?

```{r}
#| label: a6
#| eval: false
rosling |>
```

**Your finding:**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
#| label: a6-solution
rosling |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, 
             y = life_exp, 
             color = continent, 
             size = population)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_size(range = c(1, 8), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_viridis_d(guide = "none") +              # the panel title already names the continent
  facet_wrap(~ continent) +                            # one panel for each continent
  labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}",
       x = "Income per person (log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)") +
  transition_time(year)
```

The median income in Europe rises from 5,142 in 1952 to 28,054 in 2007, in Asia from 1,207 to 4,471 and in Africa from 987 to 1,452. Africa has the widest cloud in life expectancy and Oceania has 2 countries, so the Oceania panel shows only 2 points.
:::

### Step 7: Label a country while it moves

**Question.** How do we follow one country in the animation?

Create a `label` column with `mutate()` and `case_when()`: the country name for six countries (the same six as in Step 3), and `TRUE ~ ""` for all others. Draw the labels with `geom_text(aes(label = label))`. The label moves with its point in every frame. Move `size = population` from `ggplot(aes(...))` into `geom_point(aes(size = population))`. Otherwise the text size would also follow the population.

**Predict.** What does the China label do around 1962?

```{r}
#| label: a7
#| eval: false
rosling |>
```

**Your finding:**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
#| label: a7-solution
rosling |>
  mutate(label = case_when(
    country %in% c("Poland", "Sweden", "Chile", "United States", "Nigeria", "China") ~ country,   # label six countries
    TRUE ~ ""                                          # no label for all others
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, 
             y = life_exp, 
             color = continent)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = population), alpha = 0.7) +   # the size applies to the points only
  geom_text(aes(label = label), 
            color = "black",                           # one colour for all labels
            vjust = -1,                                # place the text above the point
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_size(range = c(1, 12), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}",
       x = "Income per person (log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       color = "Continent") +
  transition_time(year)
```

The China point falls to 44.5 years in 1962 and then climbs to 73.0 years in 2007, with the income rising from 400 to 4,959. Nigeria stays below 48 years in all 12 years. The Latvian data are not in this file, so Latvia cannot get a label here.
:::

## 6. Control and save the animation

### Step 8: Frames, speed and size

**Question.** How do we make the animation shorter or larger?

Put the whole plot inside `animate()`. The function `animate()` takes the plot as the first argument and settings after it: `nframes` (number of frames) and `fps` (frames per second). 50 frames at 10 frames per second last 5 seconds. Use the plot of Step 4.

The size of the animation comes from two chunk options at the top of the chunk: `#| fig-width: 8` and `#| fig-height: 5` (inches). Do not set `width` and `height` inside `animate()` in a Quarto file. Quarto reads these numbers as inches, so `width = 700` asks for a 700-inch image and R stops with the error `unable to start device 'png'`.

**Predict.** What happens with 20 frames?

```{r}
#| label: a8
#| eval: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
animate(
  rosling |>
    ggplot(
```

**Your finding:**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
#| label: a8-solution
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
animate(
  rosling |>
    ggplot(aes(x = income, 
               y = life_exp, 
               color = continent, 
               size = population)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_size(range = c(1, 12), guide = "none") +
    scale_color_viridis_d() +
    labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}",
         x = "Income per person (log scale)",
         y = "Life expectancy (years)",
         color = "Continent") +
    transition_time(year),
  nframes = 50,       # number of frames
  fps = 10            # frames per second: 50 frames last 5 seconds
)
```

With few frames the animation is short and jumps between years. With many frames it is smooth and slow.
:::

### Step 9: Save the file

**Question.** How do we keep the animation as a file for a slide or a web page?

After you have shown an animation, `anim_save("rosling.gif")` saves the last animation to a gif file in your project folder. The function needs the name of the file with the ending `.gif`. This chunk runs only on your computer, so it keeps `#| eval: false`.

```{r}
#| label: a9
#| eval: false
anim_save("rosling.gif")   # saves the last animation in the project folder
```

**Your finding:** where is the file, and how big is it?

### Step 10: An interactive animation (HTML only)

**Question.** Can the reader play the animation, stop it at one year and read the data of a country?

The package `plotly` makes graphs that react to the mouse. The function `ggplotly()` turns a ggplot into an interactive graph. Add `frame = year` and `text = country` inside `aes()`. The aesthetic `frame` tells `plotly` to build one frame for each year, with a play button and a slider. The aesthetic `text` sets the name that appears when the mouse is over a point. Wrap the whole plot in `ggplotly(..., tooltip = c("text", "x", "y"))`: `tooltip` lists what the hover box shows.

**Predict.** Do the points glide between the years, as in `gganimate`?

```{r}
#| label: a10
#| eval: false
ggplotly(
  rosling |>
```

**Your finding:**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
#| label: a10-solution
ggplotly(
  rosling |>
    ggplot(aes(x = income, 
               y = life_exp, 
               color = continent, 
               size = population, 
               text = country,         # shown when the mouse is over a point
               frame = year)) +        # one frame for each year, with a slider and a play button
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_size(range = c(1, 12), guide = "none") +
    scale_color_viridis_d(),
  tooltip = c("text", "x", "y")         # what the hover box shows
)
```

The points jump from one year to the next, without the steps in between. The reader can stop the slider at any year and read the country, income and life expectancy of each point. This works in an HTML report and not in a PDF. The next tutorial covers `plotly` from the beginning.
:::

### Check 2

A reader of your report wants to compare life expectancy of Estonia and Latvia in 1944. Which graph is better, the animation or the static line? Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The static line. In an animation the reader must remember values from an earlier frame. A static graph shows all years at once and allows a comparison at any year. An animation works best for the sequence ("first this, then that") and for a talk. A report needs the static version.
:::

## 7. Final challenge

**Question.** Animate the life expectancy of Latvia compared with the other European countries from 1900 to 2023, and decide whether the animation adds information over the static line.

Use `transition_reveal(year)`, a gray line for the other European countries and one colour for Latvia, as in the trends tutorial (Step 5c). Two functions help: `fct_relevel(name, "Latvia", after = Inf)` moves Latvia to the end of the order, so ggplot draws its line last, on top; `scale_color_manual(values = ...)` sets each colour by hand. Write one sentence about what the animation shows and one sentence about what you lose compared with a static graph.

```{r}
#| label: challenge
#| eval: false
life_long |>
```

**What the animation adds:**

**What the static graph shows better:**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="One possible answer"}
```{r}
#| label: challenge-solution
life_long |>
  filter(continent == "Europe", year >= 1900) |>
  mutate(
    highlight = case_when(
      name == "Latvia" ~ "Latvia",
      TRUE ~ "Other European countries"
    ),
    name = fct_relevel(name, "Latvia", after = Inf)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, 
             y = life_exp, 
             group = name, 
             color = highlight)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Latvia = "#d95f02", "Other European countries" = "grey80")) +
  labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_along)}",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       color = NULL) +
  transition_reveal(year)
```

The animation shows the order of events: the fall in 1944 appears after the rise in the 1920s and 1930s, and the viewer waits for it. The static graph shows the value of 26.8 years in 1944 and the level of 67.1 to 71.4 years from 1960 to 2000 at the same time, so the viewer compares both without waiting.
:::

## 8. Summary

| Question | Code | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A line that draws itself | `transition_reveal(year)` | Keeps the past, extends the line. |
| Points that move | `transition_time(year)` | One frame for each year. |
| A tail behind the points | `shadow_wake()` | Shows direction and speed. |
| Title with the year | `labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}")` | `frame_time` for `transition_time()`, `frame_along` for `transition_reveal()`. |
| Frames and speed | `animate(plot, nframes, fps)` | Controls the length. |
| Size in Quarto | chunk options `fig-width` and `fig-height` | Controls the size in inches. |
| One panel per group | `facet_wrap(~ continent)` | Separates the groups and moves all panels together. |
| Label a country that moves | new column with `case_when()`, `geom_text()` | The label follows the point. |
| Save the file | `anim_save("name.gif")` | Gives a gif for slides and web pages. |
| Play and hover in a web page | `ggplotly()` with `frame = year` | Interactive version, HTML only. |

Use animation to tell a sequence in a talk. Use a static graph when the reader must compare values.
